arraypool-rent-return.title: Reuse temporary arrays with ArrayPool<T>
arraypool-rent-return.short: Reduce repeated allocation of large temporary arrays
arraypool-rent-return.summary: ArrayPool<T> lets code rent and reuse arrays. It is useful when frequent allocation of large temporary buffers creates unnecessary GC pressure.
arraypool-rent-return.why: Rent may return an array larger than requested, and the rented array is a shared resource. Limit work to the intended range and always return the array after use.
arraypool-rent-return.tips: For sensitive data, consider Return(array, clearArray: true). Pooling every small array can add more complexity than value.

timeprovider-testable-time.title: Separate clock dependencies with TimeProvider
timeprovider-testable-time.short: Make current time replaceable for deterministic tests
timeprovider-testable-time.summary: Accepting a TimeProvider avoids hard-coding DateTime.Now or UtcNow and makes time-dependent behavior easier to test.
timeprovider-testable-time.why: Code that directly reads the current clock changes with execution time. Passing the clock as a dependency separates time retrieval from business rules.
timeprovider-testable-time.tips: Use TimeProvider.System in production and a controllable provider in tests. Keep time-zone semantics explicit for persisted values.

caller-argument-expression.title: Capture argument expressions with CallerArgumentExpression
caller-argument-expression.short: Include the caller's expression in validation diagnostics
caller-argument-expression.summary: CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute can capture the source expression passed to another parameter as text, which is useful for diagnostic helper APIs.
caller-argument-expression.why: Callers do not need to repeat an expression as a string, while failures can still report text such as count > 0.
caller-argument-expression.tips: Use the captured text for diagnostics, not as program logic that attempts to interpret source expressions.

exception-dispatch-info-rethrow.title: Preserve exceptions with ExceptionDispatchInfo
exception-dispatch-info-rethrow.short: Capture an exception and rethrow it later with its context
exception-dispatch-info-rethrow.summary: ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture stores an exception so it can later be thrown while preserving useful original exception information.
exception-dispatch-info-rethrow.why: Throwing a caught exception with throw ex can make stack information harder to interpret. ExceptionDispatchInfo is designed for delayed rethrow across a boundary.
exception-dispatch-info-rethrow.tips: If rethrowing immediately inside the same catch block, prefer throw;. Use ExceptionDispatchInfo when the exception really must be retained for later.

utf8jsonwriter-streaming.title: Write JSON incrementally with Utf8JsonWriter
utf8jsonwriter-streaming.short: Emit UTF-8 JSON with low-level control
utf8jsonwriter-streaming.summary: Utf8JsonWriter writes JSON tokens and values incrementally. It is useful for large output or when exact output structure needs direct control.
utf8jsonwriter-streaming.why: The complete object graph does not need to be assembled before output, so JSON can be built step by step.
utf8jsonwriter-streaming.tips: Keep StartObject/EndObject and similar token pairs balanced. For ordinary DTO serialization, JsonSerializer is usually simpler.

lazy-thread-safe-initialization.title: Delay initialization with Lazy<T>
lazy-thread-safe-initialization.short: Create a value once when it is first needed
lazy-thread-safe-initialization.summary: Lazy<T> represents initialization that occurs when Value is first requested. Its default behavior also accounts for concurrent initialization.
lazy-thread-safe-initialization.why: An expensive object that may never be used does not have to be created at startup, and its initialization can be centralized.
lazy-thread-safe-initialization.tips: Plan for initialization failures and object lifetime. If ordinary field initialization is sufficient, Lazy<T> may be unnecessary complexity.

lock-scope-minimize.title: Keep lock scopes as small as correctness allows
lock-scope-minimize.short: Protect shared state without holding a lock through slow work
lock-scope-minimize.summary: Waiting or performing expensive I/O while holding a lock blocks other code that needs the same lock. Keep the protected region focused on shared state.
lock-scope-minimize.why: Long lock hold times increase contention and reduce responsiveness and throughput. Copying a consistent snapshot and doing I/O afterward can help.
lock-scope-minimize.tips: Never shorten a lock by exposing an inconsistent intermediate state. First decide which state must change atomically.

arraypool-return-finally.title: Return ArrayPool<T> buffers from finally
arraypool-return-finally.short: Return rented arrays even when work throws
arraypool-return-finally.summary: A rented ArrayPool<T> buffer should be protected with try/finally so Return still runs when the operation fails.
arraypool-return-finally.why: If awaited work throws, a Return statement written afterward is skipped. Repeated missed returns undermine the benefit of pooling.
arraypool-return-finally.tips: Start the try immediately after renting and place Return in finally as a standard ownership pattern.

stream-read-partial-buffer.title: Process only the bytes returned by Stream.ReadAsync
stream-read-partial-buffer.short: Use the actual read count instead of the whole buffer
stream-read-partial-buffer.summary: Stream.ReadAsync is not required to fill the supplied buffer. Its return value is the number of bytes read by that operation.
stream-read-partial-buffer.why: The unused tail of a reused buffer may contain data from an earlier read. Processing the whole buffer can therefore consume stale bytes.
stream-read-partial-buffer.tips: Pass a range such as buffer.AsSpan(0, read), and treat a return value of zero as end of stream.

task-run-async-io.title: Do not wrap naturally asynchronous I/O in Task.Run
task-run-async-io.summary: Asynchronous I/O APIs such as HttpClient are already designed not to occupy a thread while waiting. Wrapping them in Task.Run usually adds no benefit.
task-run-async-io.why: Task.Run is primarily useful for scheduling CPU-bound work on a thread-pool thread. Wrapping asynchronous I/O adds scheduling overhead and extra code.
task-run-async-io.tips: Use Task.Run when there is a concrete CPU-bound or UI-thread reason, not as a generic wrapper around every async call.
